title: Registers, stacks and addressing modes
subtitle: Instructions are bit patterns; the CPU’s registers, flags and addressing modes decide what they can reach.

regs.title: Registers and flags
regs.body: Registers are the processor’s fastest memory. There are general-purpose ones, a program counter, a stack pointer, and a status register of flags set by the ALU: zero (result was 0), sign (negative), carry (unsigned overflow out of the top bit), parity, auxiliary carry. Conditional jumps test these flags.

stack.title: Stack organisation and reverse Polish notation
stack.body: A stack grows in memory from the stack pointer: push writes then moves the pointer, pop moves back and reads. Calls push the return address; returns pop it. A stack machine evaluates reverse Polish notation directly: push operands, and each operator pops two and pushes the result. To evaluate (A+B)×C, write A B + C × — no parentheses and no precedence rules needed.
stack.steps: Evaluate 3 4 + 2 × in RPN with a stack. Push 3, push 4, then + pops both and pushes 7. Push 2; × pops 2 and 7, pushes 14.

formats.title: Instruction formats
formats.body: An instruction word holds an opcode and zero to three operand fields. Three-address instructions (ADD R1,R2,R3) are compact in program length; two-address overwrite one source; one-address use an implicit accumulator; zero-address use the stack. Fewer addresses make each instruction shorter but need more instructions.
formats.steps: Compute X = (A+B)×(C+D) on each machine type. Three-address: ADD R1,A,B; ADD R2,C,D; MUL X,R1,R2 → 3 instructions. One-address (accumulator): LOAD A; ADD B; STORE T; LOAD C; ADD D; MUL T; STORE X → 7.

modes.title: Addressing modes
modes.body: How does an instruction say where its data is? Immediate: the value is in the instruction (MVI A,05H). Direct: the instruction holds the address (LDA 2050H). Register: the operand is in a register (MOV A,B). Register indirect: a register holds the address (MOV A,M uses HL). Indexed/base-relative: address = register + offset, ideal for arrays. Each trades instruction length and speed for flexibility.

interrupts.title: Interrupts
interrupts.body: An interrupt diverts the CPU to an interrupt service routine (ISR) when a device needs attention, an error occurs, or a timer fires. Between instructions the CPU checks for one; if accepted it saves the program counter and flags, jumps to the ISR (found through a vector table), runs it, and returns to exactly where it left off.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Flags record ALU outcomes; jumps read them.
  • Stacks serve calls, returns and RPN evaluation.
  • Fewer address fields mean shorter instructions but more of them.
  • Addressing modes choose how an operand is found.
